lesson.title: Measuring Voltage: Touching In Without Breaking Anything
lesson.summary: Measuring voltage with a multimeter means connecting the meter in parallel across the two points you want to compare, never breaking the circuit to do it.
lesson.body:
Voltage is always a difference measured between two points, so measuring it means placing your multimeter's two probes on those two points, in parallel with whatever is between them, while the circuit continues to operate exactly as it was. Set the multimeter's dial to the voltage function, choosing DC or AC to match the kind of signal you expect, touch the red probe to one point and the black probe to the other, and read the number on the display. You do not cut a wire, remove a component, or otherwise interrupt the circuit; you simply touch in at two points and let the meter sense the potential difference between them.

This works cleanly because a good voltmeter is built with an extremely high internal resistance, typically several megaohms, so that almost no current flows through the meter itself when you connect it. Since it draws essentially no current, it does not meaningfully disturb the very voltage it is trying to measure. Suppose you have a resistor in a simple series circuit and you want to check the voltage across it. You place the red probe on one leg of the resistor and the black probe on the other leg, without disconnecting either leg from the circuit, and the meter reads, say, 3.3 volts. That reading should match what you would calculate using the resistor's value and the current through it, giving you a way to check your understanding of the circuit against a real measurement.

The habit to build here, touch across two points, never break the connection, is the opposite of what you need for measuring current, which is why the two are easy to confuse and worth contrasting directly.
